The ATO splits the reporting on that basis: "If you report RFBA through STP there are two amount fields - 'exempt' and 'non-exempt'." The exemption reaches a defined set of employers - registered public benevolent institutions, government bodies whose employee works in or for a public hospital, registered health promotion charities and public ambulance services - so a figure here marks the payer as one of them, and RFB_TXBL_AMT holds the equivalent for everyone else.
value_definition: A dollar amount grossed up at the lower, type 2 rate, which is one divided by one minus the FBT rate, or 1.8868 while that rate is 47 per cent. It is reported only where the total taxable value of an employee's reportable benefits exceeds $2,000 in the FBT year, and it is reported in full even where the benefits exceed the employer's capping threshold.
limitation: The word exempt describes the employer's FBT position, not any relief for the employee: the benefit is still reported and still counts in the income tests that use it. A zero also carries no information about benefits received, only that this payer is outside section 57A, and the $2,000 floor censors small amounts entirely, so the column cannot measure low-value benefits.
rationale: The FBT guide chapter on reportable fringe benefits names the two STP amount fields, lists the section 57A entities and sets out the threshold and gross-up, which is precisely the distinction this column carries.
evidence_quote: If you report RFBA through STP there are two amount fields - 'exempt' and 'non-exempt'.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Reportable Fringe Benefits Exempt Amount - Event payment' with a dollar domain inferred from the name, and never said what the amount is exempt from or whose status the word describes.

value_domain: Reportable fringe benefits amount, employer not exempt under section 57A (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Fringe benefits tax - a guide for employers, chapter 5 Reportable fringe benefits
variable_description: The grossed-up value of an employee's reportable fringe benefits where the employer is an ordinary, FBT-paying one. It is the non-exempt half of the pair the ATO describes when it says the two STP fields represent "RFBA reportable by an employer that is exempt from FBT under section 57A of the FBTAA, and RFBA reportable by an employer that is not exempt". The custodian's word taxable refers to the employer's liability, not the employee's: the guide is explicit that the amount "is not included in the employee's assessable income" and is instead used to test eligibility for transfer payments, the Medicare levy surcharge, the private health insurance rebate and Division 293 tax.
value_definition: A dollar amount, grossed up at the type 2 rate, covering benefits provided over the FBT year of 1 April to 31 March and reported in the income year that ends straight after it.
limitation: The twelve months it describes are not the twelve months of the wages beside it, because the FBT year runs three months ahead of the financial year, so this column and gross pay on the same row cover different periods. An employee who moves between exempt and non-exempt duties in one year can also carry an amount in both fringe benefit columns, and adding them is only valid if that is understood.
rationale: The FBT guide defines both STP fields by the employer's section 57A status, states that the reported amount is not assessable income, and sets out the FBT year and the income year it is reported against.
evidence_quote: Even though a reportable fringe benefits amount is shown on an online STP Employment income statement or on a payment summary, it is not included in the employee's assessable income.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Reportable Fringe Benefits Taxable Amount - Event payment' with an inferred dollar domain, which invited the reader to treat the amount as taxable income of the employee.

value_domain: ASGS 2021 Statistical Area Level 2 code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 2
variable_description: The SA2 the ABS geocoded from the payee address on this pay event, and the level most non-Census statistics are published at. ABS defines SA2s as "medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1 (SA1s)" whose "purpose is to represent a community that interacts together socially and economically", which makes this the practical column for setting payroll earnings against regional population, income or labour force estimates. STP_MESHBLOCK_ABS on the same row is finer and LGA_ASGS_2022 is the administrative alternative.
value_definition: A nine-digit hierarchical code: one digit for state or territory, two for SA4, two for SA3 and four for the SA2. ASGS Edition 3 has 2,473 of them, including 19 non-spatial special purpose codes such as Migratory - Offshore - Shipping and No Usual Address.
limitation: It is where the employee lives, not where the job sits, so an SA2 total built from this column counts residents who are employed rather than jobs located in the area, and the two differ most in commuter suburbs and in city centres. The address is also the one the payroll holds, so a person who moved without telling their employer is coded to the old area until the record is updated.
rationale: The custodian's label reads 'Geocoded SA2', which fixes the classification, and the ASGS Edition 3 chapter gives the definition, the purpose, the coding structure and the count.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 2 (SA2s) are medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1 (SA1s). Their purpose is to represent a community that interacts together socially and economically.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Geocoded SA2' and inferred an SA2 domain from the variable name, so it never warned that the geography is residential rather than workplace.

value_domain: Job pay sequence key (derived, hashed)
value_source: ATO, Single Touch Payroll Phase 2 employer reporting guidelines, Changing your payroll solution or employees' Payroll IDs
variable_description: The key for one payroll stream within a job, built from the employee key, the payroll ID, the branch number and the payroll software identifier. It is the same combination the ATO uses to decide what an employee sees: "Your payroll solution will generate your STP report for your pay cycle by ABN, branch and BMS ID. We use this combination of information, together with the Payroll IDs you report, to identify when we need to display a separate income statement to a taxpayer." It is therefore finer than EMPLOYEE_KEY, which identifies the job, and it is the level at which year-to-date amounts accumulate.
value_definition: An opaque derived identifier with no meaning in its own value. Its components are the employee key plus the payroll ID, branch number and business management software identifier the employer reported.
limitation: A new key does not mean a new job. Changing payroll software, restructuring branches or reissuing payroll IDs mints a new key for the same person in the same employment, so counting distinct keys overstates job mobility. Where an employer moves year-to-date balances by the zeroing-out method, the retired key is left showing zeros rather than the amounts actually paid under it.
rationale: The custodian defines the key as employee key plus payroll ID, branch number and BMS ID, and the guidelines chapter on changing payroll solutions explains what that combination does, when it changes and what happens to the old stream's balances.
evidence_quote: Your payroll solution will generate your STP report for your pay cycle by ABN, branch and BMS ID. We use this combination of information, together with the Payroll IDs you report, to identify when we need to display a separate income statement to a taxpayer.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's formula for the key with an opaque-identifier domain inferred from the name, and said nothing about the events that create a new key for an unchanged job.

value_domain: Employer super liability, year to date (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Single Touch Payroll Phase 2 employer reporting guidelines, Other components of your STP reporting
variable_description: The compulsory super the employer owes for this employee so far in the year, taken from payroll rather than from a fund. The ATO asks for "your YTD employer super liability for each employee in the STP report (super type L)", while the money itself travels separately: "You must continue to report and pay your employees' super entitlements through your existing SuperStream solution." The amount is the super guarantee liability accrued on ordinary time earnings, which is why PYR_SPNTN_CNTRBTN_RPRTBL_AMT beside it holds only the negotiated extra above this.
value_definition: A cumulative dollar amount within the financial year, calculated in payroll as the super guarantee percentage of ordinary time earnings, or the higher rate where an award or agreement sets one.
limitation: A liability is not a contribution. Nothing here shows whether the money reached a fund, or reached it on time, so unpaid super looks identical to paid super. Before 30 June 2026 an employer could satisfy the obligation by reporting ordinary time earnings instead of the liability, so a zero can mean the payer reported the other measure rather than that no super was owed.
rationale: The guidelines chapter on other components states the super reporting obligation, names the two alternatives available to employers and separates STP reporting from the SuperStream payment channel, which is the distinction a reader has to know before using this column.
evidence_quote: You must continue to report and pay your employees' super entitlements through your existing SuperStream solution
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Superannuation Guarantee Employer Contribution Amount - Event payment' with an inferred dollar domain, leaving the reader to assume the figure was money received by a fund.

value_domain: ASGS state and territory code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
variable_description: The state or territory on the pay event address, coded to the ABS geography. Its label differs from the three columns beside it, which are titled geocoded LGA, SA2 and mesh block, so it appears to be the state carried in the reported structured address rather than a product of the geocoder. ABS notes that "in general, the total area of each State and Territory, including their offshore islands, is used for statistical purposes as a separate geographic area in the ASGS", with the small external territories collapsed into one Other Territories category.
value_definition: A one-digit code: 1 New South Wales, 2 Victoria, 3 Queensland, 4 South Australia, 5 Western Australia, 6 Tasmania, 7 Northern Territory, 8 Australian Capital Territory and 9 Other Territories.
limitation: It should not be assumed to agree with the leading digit of the SA2 code on the same row: a reported state that is wrong or out of date survives in this column, while the geocoded columns follow the matched address or stay empty. Code 9 also bundles Jervis Bay Territory with Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Norfolk Island, so those jurisdictions cannot be separated.
rationale: The ABS chapter defines the state and territory level of ASGS Edition 3 and gives the one-digit codes this column uses. That it comes from the reported structured address rather than the geocoder is read from the custodian's label, which names the structured geographic address field while its neighbours say geocoded, and is not separately published.
evidence_quote: In general, the total area of each State and Territory, including their offshore islands, is used for statistical purposes as a separate geographic area in the ASGS.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Structured Geographic Address State Code' with a state domain inferred from the variable name, and did not flag that this column and the geocoded ones can disagree.

value_domain: ABS mesh block code
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Mesh Blocks
variable_description: The mesh block containing the payee address, the finest geography carried on the pay event and the one every other area on the row is built from. ABS describes them as "the smallest geographic areas defined by the ABS" which "form the building blocks for the larger regions of the Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS)", designed "where possible to contain between 30 and 60 dwellings". Because they are so small, ABS publishes very little at this level, so the column is most useful for aggregating payroll records to a custom area rather than for reading on its own.
value_definition: A mesh block code from ASGS Edition 3, which contains 368,286 mesh blocks including 114 non-spatial special purpose codes for populations that are hard to place, such as people in transit or with no fixed address.
limitation: The column name carries no ASGS edition, unlike SA2_ASGS_2021 and LGA_ASGS_2022 beside it, so the vintage has to be confirmed in the extract before joining to boundaries or to Census counts. A mesh block is also not a dwelling or a household: two employees sharing a code are neighbours at best, and the small population behind each code makes any count built directly on it disclosive.
rationale: The custodian's label reads 'Geocoded Meshblock', and the ASGS Edition 3 mesh block chapter gives the definition, the design target and the counts, including the non-spatial codes.
evidence_quote: Mesh Blocks are the smallest geographic areas defined by the ABS and form the building blocks for the larger regions of the Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS).
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Geocoded Meshblock' and was tagged with a payroll topic rather than a geography domain, so nothing explained the size of the unit or the missing edition.

value_domain: PLIDA person linkage key (synthetic)
value_source: ABS, Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA), data and legislation
variable_description: The person key that ties an employee's payroll history to the rest of PLIDA, derived from the scrambled identifier the ATO holds for the payee. ABS records the collection as an enduring ATO linkage, "Single Touch Payroll, from 2020-21", carrying "Information about employees' salaries and wages, pay as you go (PAYG) withholding and superannuation as reported through the Single Touch Payroll system". Within STP it is the column that gathers a person's pay events, jobs and termination payments together, while EMPLOYEE_KEY and SEQUENCE_KEY keep their several concurrent jobs and payroll streams apart.
value_definition: An opaque synthetic person identifier, one value per person, repeated on every row that belongs to them and shared with the other PLIDA collections linked through the Person Linkage Spine.
limitation: It identifies the payee as the employer reported them, so it inherits the employer's records: a person reported without a tax file number, or under someone else's, either fails to link to the spine or attaches to the wrong person. It also carries no employer, so counting rows per person counts pay events rather than jobs, and it says nothing about whether the person worked in a month with no pay event.
rationale: The ABS page listing PLIDA's linked collections names the STP linkage, its period and its content, and the spine is what makes this column joinable to the other collections; it is the fact the entry needed and lacked.
evidence_quote: Single Touch Payroll, from 2020-21. Information about employees' salaries and wages, pay as you go (PAYG) withholding and superannuation as reported through the Single Touch Payroll system.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence about a synthetic identifier derived from the payee's scrambled identifier and inferred an opaque-identifier domain, without saying what it can be joined to or how linkage can fail.

value_domain: Total PAYG withholding, year to date (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Single Touch Payroll Phase 2 employer reporting guidelines, Tax that has been withheld or paid
variable_description: The tax the employer has held back from this employee's pay so far in the year and remitted to the ATO. The obligation is reported by category: "You must report the amounts you withhold from payments you make to employees. You must include separate YTD amounts you have withheld from each income type (and for income types that require a country code, for each combination of income type and country code)." This column carries the main salary and wages total, with VA_TOTL_AMT, LABR_HIR_TOTL_AMT, WHM_TOTL_AMT and OTHR_SPCFD_TOTL_AMT holding the withholding for the other income types.
value_definition: A cumulative dollar amount within the financial year, remitted under the pay as you go withholding system and credited against the employee's assessment.
limitation: Withholding is not tax paid. It is an instalment set by tax tables and by what the employee declared to the payer, so a person who claimed the wrong threshold or has several jobs can be well over or under, and the difference only settles on assessment. For foreign employment income the employer reports the residual after foreign tax, so the column understates the total collected on that income.
rationale: The guidelines chapter on withholding states what employers must report, the year-to-date and per-income-type structure, and the foreign employment income rule that makes the reported figure a residual.
evidence_quote: You must report the amounts you withhold from payments you make to employees. You must include separate YTD amounts you have withheld from each income type (and for income types that require a country code, for each combination of income type and country code).
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Total PAYGW Amount - Event payment' with a dollar domain inferred from the name, so nothing distinguished it from the other withholding columns on the row.

value_domain: PAYG withholding under a voluntary agreement, year to date (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Payments to contractors under a voluntary agreement
variable_description: Tax withheld year to date from an independent contractor under a voluntary agreement, so a figure here marks the worker as a contractor rather than an employee. Withholding from contractors is normally optional: "you and a contract worker (payee) can enter into a voluntary agreement to withhold an amount of tax from each payment you make to them", and the rate is the contractor's Commissioner's instalment rate, or "a flat rate of 20% (if the instalment rate is not known or is less than 20%)". The amount is worked out on the invoiced sum with any GST taken out first.
value_definition: A cumulative dollar amount within the financial year, calculated on GST-exclusive payments at the agreed instalment or flat rate rather than from the tax tables used for wages.
limitation: The column is a poor census of contracting. A voluntary agreement is optional and can be ended in writing by either party at any time, and it cannot be used where the payment already falls under another withholding category such as labour hire, so most contractors never appear here at all. A zero therefore says nothing about whether contract work was done.
rationale: The ATO page defines the voluntary agreement, states who it covers, sets the withholding rates and excludes payments already covered by another withholding category, which is what makes the column a selected slice rather than a measure of contracting.
evidence_quote: Voluntary agreements can't be used where the payment is already covered by another PAYG withholding category, such as payments to employees or under labour hire arrangements.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Voluntary Agreement Total PAYGW Amount - Event payment' with an inferred dollar domain, and did not say that the row describes a contractor or how the rate is set.

value_domain: PAYG withholding, year to date (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Single Touch Payroll Phase 2 employer reporting guidelines, Tax that has been withheld or paid
variable_description: A year-to-date withholding total on the pay event, sitting alongside the withholding columns that are keyed to a payment or income type. Its label is the only one in the family to say year to date, although in STP every amount is cumulative: the ATO requires "separate YTD amounts you have withheld from each income type". The monthly tables span the move to STP Phase 2, which employers began from 1 January 2022 and which recast withholding from the old payment summary categories onto income types, so which of these columns is populated depends on the month and on when the payer transitioned.
value_definition: A cumulative dollar amount of pay as you go withholding within the financial year, reset at the start of each year.
limitation: The label does not say which payments it covers, so it must not be added to TAX_WHELD_TOTL_AMT or to the income-type withholding columns before checking, month by month, which of them are filled; double counting a person's tax is the obvious error. The reading of it as the successor to the payment summary style totals is inferred from the column set and the timing of the Phase 2 change, not published.
rationale: The guidelines establish that STP withholding is reported as year-to-date amounts split by income type, which is what this column and its neighbours hold. The relationship between the several withholding columns is assembled from the label set and the Phase 1 to Phase 2 change rather than quoted from a source.
evidence_quote: You must report the amounts you withhold from payments you make to employees. You must include separate YTD amounts you have withheld from each income type.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Year To Date Withheld Amount - Event payment' with a dollar domain inferred from the name, and gave no warning about its overlap with the other withholding columns.

value_domain: PAYG withholding on working holiday maker income, year to date (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Single Touch Payroll Phase 2 employer reporting guidelines, Income types
variable_description: Tax withheld year to date from pay the employer assigned to the working holiday maker income type, which exists because that income is taxed on its own scale. The ATO ties the type to the visa: "Use this income type when you're making payments to a person that is a working holiday maker. This means they're a temporary visitor to Australia holding a subclass 417 (working holiday) or subclass 462 (work and holiday) visa." A nonzero value therefore dates a period of visa status as well as a tax amount, and INCM_WHM_GRS_AMT on the same row carries the matching gross.
value_definition: A cumulative dollar amount within the financial year, withheld at the working holiday maker scale, which begins at 15 cents in the dollar on the first band of income rather than at the resident tax-free threshold.
limitation: It covers only the part of the year the person was reported as a working holiday maker. Someone who moves onto a different visa mid-year has the rest of their pay reported as ordinary salary and wages, so this column understates their tax and cannot be read as their annual total. It also does not distinguish subclass 417 from 462, and it is the country code, not this figure, that records nationality.
rationale: The guidelines define the working holiday maker income type by visa subclass and explain that the type exists because the income is taxed differently, which is what this withholding column measures. The 15 per cent first band is the ATO's published working holiday maker rate scale.
evidence_quote: Use this income type when you're making payments to a person that is a working holiday maker. This means they're a temporary visitor to Australia holding a subclass 417 (working holiday) or subclass 462 (work and holiday) visa.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Working Holiday Maker Total PAYGW Amount - Event payment' with an inferred dollar domain, so it did not say what a working holiday maker is or that the column covers only part of a mixed year.
